questions.title: JUnit 5 Essentials
questions.question: What are the key features of JUnit 5 and how do you structure unit tests?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **JUnit 5 = JUnit Platform + JUnit Jupiter + JUnit Vintage**
- **`@Test`, `@BeforeEach`, `@AfterEach`, `@BeforeAll`, `@AfterAll`**
- **`@DisplayName`, `@Nested`, `@ParameterizedTest` for organization**
- **AssertJ for fluent assertions — more readable than JUnit's built-in**
- **AAA pattern: Arrange, Act, Assert — every test follows this**
- **Red flag:** test methods that test multiple behaviors — one behavior per test

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
JUnit 5 is the current standard for Java unit testing, consisting of three modules: JUnit Platform (the foundation), JUnit Jupiter (the programming model — the annotations you use), and JUnit Vintage (for running JUnit 4 tests). Spring Boot includes it by default.

Every test should follow the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern: set up data and dependencies, invoke the method under test, then assert the expected outcome. Tests should be independent — each `@Test` method should work in isolation, with setup in `@BeforeEach` and teardown in `@AfterEach`.

`@Nested` classes group related tests within a test class, improving readability. `@ParameterizedTest` with `@MethodSource` or `@CsvSource` runs the same test logic with multiple inputs — ideal for boundary conditions and equivalence partitions.

questions.title: Test Coverage and Test Design
questions.question: What should you focus on for good test coverage in a service layer?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Coverage metric is a proxy, not the goal — 100% coverage can still miss important cases**
- **Focus on: happy path, error paths, boundary conditions, edge cases**
- **Equivalence partitioning: group inputs with same behavior, test one from each**
- **Branch coverage: every `if-else` path exercised**
- **Don't test: getters/setters, framework code, trivial delegation**
- **Red flag:** chasing 100% coverage by testing trivial code while missing business logic branches

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Good test coverage isn't about hitting a percentage number — it's about covering the behaviors that matter. For a service method, you need to cover: the happy path (normal successful execution), all error paths (exceptions thrown, validation failures), and boundary conditions (minimum/maximum values, empty collections, null inputs).

Use equivalence partitioning: group input values by the behavior they produce, then test one representative from each group. For an age field, you might have groups: negative (invalid), 0-17 (minor), 18-64 (adult), 65+ (senior). One test per group suffices unless the boundaries themselves are what's being tested.

Don't write tests for trivial code: Lombok-generated getters/setters, Spring dependency injection configuration, or framework behavior you don't control. Focus tests on code paths with logic, branching, and business rules.

questions.question: What is the difference between unit, integration, and end-to-end tests, and when should you use each?
questions.title: Unit vs Integration vs End-to-End Testing
questions.direct_answer: Unit tests verify individual methods/classes in isolation using mocks, run in milliseconds. Integration tests verify components working together (e.g., controller + service + real DB), run in seconds. E2E tests verify full user journeys through the deployed application, run in minutes. The testing pyramid recommends many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few E2E tests.

sections.title: The Testing Pyramid Isn't About Ratios — It's About Feedback Speed vs Confidence
sections.content:
The testing pyramid puts unit tests at the base, integration tests in the middle, and end-to-end tests at the top. Most explanations focus on quantity ("more unit tests, fewer E2E tests"), but the real insight is about **feedback loops and failure diagnosis.**

A unit test runs in milliseconds, tests one class in isolation, and when it fails, tells you exactly what broke. An integration test runs in seconds, verifies that components work together (Spring context, database, HTTP), and when it fails, might point to the component or the interaction. An end-to-end test runs in minutes, verifies the full user flow, and when it fails, tells you *something* is broken — but finding what requires investigation.

The pyramid's shape reflects this trade-off: you want **fast, precise tests as the foundation** and **slow, broad tests as verification.** The anti-pattern is the ice cream cone — mostly E2E tests with few unit tests. This means every failure triggers a 15-minute investigation instead of a 15-second method name. Tests become so slow that developers stop running them locally, and CI becomes the only feedback loop.

Unit tests give you speed. Integration tests give you confidence that components connect correctly. E2E tests give you confidence that the system works as a user would experience it.

sections.title: Unit vs Integration vs E2E — What Each Level Proves
sections.content:
| Aspect | Unit Test | Integration Test | E2E Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scope | One class/method | Multiple components + infrastructure | Full system through UI/API |
| Dependencies | Mocked | Real (DB, Spring context, HTTP) | Everything real |
| Speed | Milliseconds | Seconds | Minutes |
| Failure diagnosis | Exact method | Component or interaction | "Something is broken" |
| Frameworks | JUnit 5 + Mockito | `@SpringBootTest`, `@DataJpaTest` | Selenium, Playwright, REST Assured |
| When to write | Every business rule | Database queries, API contracts, configs | Critical user journeys only |
| Maintenance cost | Low | Medium | High (brittle, environment-dependent) |

The table reveals the cost curve: E2E tests are the most expensive to write, the slowest to run, and the hardest to diagnose. Investing heavily in E2E over unit tests maximizes cost while minimizing feedback speed.

sections.title: What to Test at Each Level — The Decision Framework
sections.content:
**Unit test when:** the logic is in your code — business rules, calculations, transformations, validation. If the method takes inputs and produces outputs without external dependencies, it's a unit test. This includes services with mocked repositories, mappers, validators, and utility classes.

**Integration test when:** correctness depends on how components interact — JPA queries returning correct results, REST endpoints accepting the right request format, Spring Security denying unauthorized requests, configuration loading correctly. The test verifies the *wiring*, not the logic.

**E2E test when:** you need confidence that the full system works for critical user journeys — login, checkout, payment, onboarding. Keep these to 5-15 scenarios that cover the most important flows. Every additional E2E test adds maintenance cost and CI time.

The practical rule: **if you can test it with a unit test, don't write an integration test.** If the integration test covers it, don't add an E2E test. Push testing to the lowest level that still gives you confidence.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Unit tests verify one class in isolation with mocked dependencies — they run in milliseconds and tell you exactly what broke. Integration tests verify that components work together with real infrastructure — Spring context, database, HTTP. E2E tests verify complete user flows through the entire system.

The pyramid isn't about having "more unit tests" — it's about **feedback speed vs confidence.** A failing unit test points to the exact method in seconds. A failing E2E test says "something is broken" and takes minutes to diagnose.

The anti-pattern is the ice cream cone — mostly E2E tests, few unit tests. Tests become so slow that developers stop running them locally, and CI becomes the only feedback loop. My rule: if you can test it with a unit test, don't write an integration test. Push testing to the lowest level that still gives you confidence.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Unit tests run in milliseconds; E2E tests run in minutes** — the pyramid reflects feedback speed, not just quantity; push testing to the lowest level that gives confidence.
- **The ice cream cone anti-pattern (mostly E2E) kills developer productivity** — tests become too slow to run locally; CI becomes the only feedback, and developers stop running tests before commits.
- **Integration tests verify wiring, not logic** — JPA queries, REST endpoint contracts, security rules, configuration; if correctness depends on component interaction, it's an integration test.
- **E2E tests should cover only critical user journeys** — 5-15 scenarios (login, checkout, payment); each additional E2E test adds maintenance cost and CI time with diminishing returns.
- **A failing unit test names the broken method; a failing E2E test says "something is broken"** — diagnosis time is the hidden cost; 100 fast unit tests give better ROI than 10 slow E2E tests.

questions.question: What is @SpringBootTest and when would you use its slice variants like @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest instead?
questions.title: @SpringBootTest and Its Slice Variants
questions.direct_answer: @SpringBootTest loads the full application context and is great for true integration tests, but is slow. Slice annotations load only the relevant portion: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers, filters, security), @DataJpaTest loads only the persistence layer (repositories, entities, DataSource). Use slices to get faster, more focused tests without bootstrapping the entire context.

sections.title: @SpringBootTest Loads Everything — That's Why It's Slow and Why Slices Exist
sections.content:
`@SpringBootTest` starts the full Spring application context — every bean, every auto-configuration, every component scan. This gives maximum fidelity but at a cost: context startup takes 5-30 seconds depending on the application. For a project with 200 tests all using `@SpringBootTest`, the test suite runs for 30+ minutes.

**Test slices** load only the parts of the context relevant to what you're testing. `@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)` loads the web layer — controller, filters, converters — but not services, repositories, or database connections. `@DataJpaTest` loads JPA repositories and an embedded H2 database but not controllers or services.

The performance difference is dramatic. A `@WebMvcTest` starts in under 2 seconds. The same test with `@SpringBootTest` takes 10-15 seconds because it loads the entire application including database connections, message brokers, and scheduled tasks that the test doesn't need.

Spring caches application contexts across tests with the same configuration — but slices with different `@MockBean` annotations create different cache keys, triggering new context creation. Minimizing distinct `@MockBean` combinations across test classes keeps context caching effective.

sections.title: Test Slice Selection — What Each Annotation Loads
sections.content:
| Annotation | What it loads | What it excludes | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@SpringBootTest` | Everything | Nothing | Full integration tests, app startup verification |
| `@WebMvcTest` | Controllers, filters, `@ControllerAdvice` | Services, repositories, DB | Controller request/response testing |
| `@DataJpaTest` | JPA repos, `EntityManager`, H2/Testcontainers | Controllers, services | Repository query verification |
| `@WebFluxTest` | WebFlux controllers | Everything else | Reactive controller testing |
| `@JsonTest` | Jackson `ObjectMapper` | Everything else | JSON serialization/deserialization |
| `@RestClientTest` | `RestTemplate` / `WebClient` with mock server | Everything else | External API client testing |

The pattern: **use the narrowest slice that covers what you're testing.** If you're testing a controller's request mapping and validation, `@WebMvcTest` is faster and more focused than `@SpringBootTest`. If you're testing a JPA query, `@DataJpaTest` loads only what the repository needs.

sections.title: When @SpringBootTest Is Actually the Right Choice
Test Profile and Property Overrides — Isolating Test Configuration
sections.content:
Test slices often need different configuration than production. `@TestPropertySource(properties = "spring.jpa.show-sql=true")` overrides individual properties. `@ActiveProfiles("test")` activates a test-specific `application-test.yml` with test database URLs, disabled scheduling, and mock external service endpoints.

The hierarchy matters: `@TestPropertySource` overrides profile properties, which override `application.yml`. This lets you keep most configuration in the default file and override only what's test-specific.

One pattern that prevents test configuration drift: create a `src/test/resources/application-test.yml` that disables everything tests don't need — scheduled tasks (`spring.task.scheduling.enabled=false`), actuator endpoints, and Kafka auto-configuration. Tests start faster because Spring skips auto-configuration for components that aren't part of the test.

For `@DataJpaTest`, properties like `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop` ensure a clean schema per test run. Combined with `@Transactional` rollback, this gives complete test isolation without manual cleanup scripts.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@SpringBootTest` loads the full application context — every bean, every auto-configuration. It gives maximum fidelity but takes 10-30 seconds to start. Test slices like `@WebMvcTest` and `@DataJpaTest` load only the relevant portion, starting in under 2 seconds.

`@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)` loads just the controller layer — no services, no repositories, no database. You mock dependencies with `@MockBean`. `@DataJpaTest` loads JPA repositories with an embedded database — no controllers.

The rule: **use the narrowest slice that covers what you're testing.** Reserve `@SpringBootTest` for smoke tests and cross-cutting integration tests — maybe 10-20% of your suite. The rest should use slices.

One thing that trips people up: Spring caches contexts, but each unique `@MockBean` combination creates a new cache key. Minimizing distinct mock combinations across test classes keeps caching effective and the suite fast.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@SpringBootTest` takes 10-30 seconds; `@WebMvcTest` takes under 2 seconds** — the full context loads every bean including database, messaging, and scheduled tasks that your controller test doesn't need.
- **Each unique `@MockBean` combination creates a new context cache key** — 10 test classes with different mock sets means 10 context startups; standardize mock combinations across tests to maximize caching.
- **`@DataJpaTest` auto-configures an embedded H2 database** — add `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` to use Testcontainers instead of H2 for realistic SQL testing.
- **`webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT` starts a real HTTP server** — tests the full HTTP stack including filters and content negotiation; use `TestRestTemplate` instead of `MockMvc` for these tests.
- **80% of tests should use slices; 20% should use `@SpringBootTest`** — if you're testing a controller, use `@WebMvcTest`; if you're testing a query, use `@DataJpaTest`; reserve full context for smoke and cross-cutting tests.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Mock, @Spy, and @MockBean in Mockito/Spring Boot tests?
questions.title: Mockito: @Mock vs @Spy vs @MockBean
questions.direct_answer: @Mock creates a pure Mockito mock — all methods return default values unless stubbed; used in plain unit tests. @Spy wraps a real object, delegating to real methods unless overridden; useful when you want mostly real behaviour with one method stubbed. @MockBean creates a Mockito mock AND registers it in the Spring application context, replacing any existing bean of that type — required in @WebMvcTest and @SpringBootTest when you need to stub a Spring-managed dependency.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the distinction between plain Mockito and Spring-managed mocks, and when a spy is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @MockBean in plain unit tests (unnecessary and slow — it requires a Spring context to start) or using @Mock when you need Spring to inject the mock
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @MockBean causes the Spring context to be recreated if it wasn't already created with that mock, which can slow down suites — so centralise @MockBean usage in base test classes

sections.title: @Mock Is Fast and Free — @MockBean Loads Spring and Should Be Your Last Resort
sections.content:
Three annotations create test doubles in Java testing, and using the wrong one in the wrong context either slows your tests or makes them unreliable.

**`@Mock`** (Mockito) creates a mock object without Spring. It's fast — no context loading, no bean registration. Use it in plain unit tests where you control all dependencies through constructor injection. The mock returns defaults (null for objects, 0 for primitives, empty for collections) unless you configure behavior with `when().thenReturn()`.

**`@MockBean`** (Spring Boot Test) creates a mock AND registers it in the Spring application context, replacing the real bean. It requires a Spring context to exist — meaning it only works with `@SpringBootTest` or test slices. This is powerful but expensive: adding `@MockBean` in a test class may invalidate the cached context, forcing a full context reload.

**`@Spy`** (Mockito) wraps a real object — real method calls execute unless you override them with `when().thenReturn()`. This is useful when most of the object's behavior should be real but you need to override one specific method (e.g., a method that calls an external service).

The mistake: using `@MockBean` in plain unit tests. If you're testing a service with a mocked repository and no Spring context needed, `@Mock` with `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` is 100x faster.

sections.title: @Mock vs @Spy vs @MockBean — The Decision Matrix
sections.content:
| Aspect | `@Mock` | `@Spy` | `@MockBean` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Framework | Mockito | Mockito | Spring Boot Test |
| Spring context required | No | No | Yes |
| Creates | Fake object, all methods stubbed | Wraps real object | Mock registered as Spring bean |
| Default behavior | Returns null/0/empty | Calls real methods | Returns null/0/empty |
| Speed | Instant | Instant | Requires context startup |
| Use when | Unit testing with DI | Need mostly real behavior | Integration test needs mock in context |
| Context cache impact | None | None | May invalidate cached context |

The table makes the cost clear: `@Mock` and `@Spy` are free. `@MockBean` potentially triggers a multi-second context reload.

How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@Mock` creates a Mockito mock without Spring — instant, free, perfect for unit tests. `@MockBean` creates a mock AND registers it in the Spring context, replacing the real bean. It's powerful but expensive — it requires a context and may invalidate the cached context, forcing a full reload.

The mistake is using `@MockBean` in plain unit tests. If you're testing a service with mocked dependencies and no Spring context, `@Mock` with `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` runs 100x faster.

`@Spy` wraps a real object — real methods execute unless you override them. It's for the rare case where you need mostly real behavior but need to stub one method that calls an external service.

My rule: **`@Mock` by default, `@Spy` when you need partial real behavior, `@MockBean` only when the test requires a Spring context and you need to replace a specific bean.**

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Mock` needs no Spring context — `@MockBean` requires one** — using `@MockBean` in a plain unit test forces unnecessary context loading; use `@Mock` + `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` instead.
- **`@MockBean` can invalidate the context cache** — each unique `@MockBean` combination creates a new cache key; different mock sets across test classes multiply context startups.
- **`@Spy` calls real methods unless overridden** — `@Mock` returns defaults for everything; `@Spy` executes the actual implementation; override specific methods with `doReturn().when()` for partial mocking.
- **`@InjectMocks` creates the class and injects `@Mock` fields** — eliminates manual constructor calls; works with constructor injection, setter injection, and field injection.
- **Use `doReturn().when()` instead of `when().thenReturn()` with spies** — `when().thenReturn()` calls the real method before stubbing (side effects execute); `doReturn().when()` avoids executing the real method entirely.

questions.direct_answer: Use @DataJpaTest with @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE) to prevent Spring from replacing your DataSource with H2. Declare a PostgreSQLContainer as a static @Container field and use @DynamicPropertySource to inject the container's JDBC URL, username, and password into the Spring context before it starts. This gives you tests that run against real Postgres with the same dialect, indexes, and constraints as production.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE) — without it Spring replaces your DataSource with H2 even when Testcontainers is configured

sections.title: H2 Lies About Your Queries — Testcontainers Runs the Real Database
sections.content:
`@DataJpaTest` auto-configures an embedded H2 database by default. This is fast but deceptive — H2's SQL dialect differs from MySQL and PostgreSQL in subtle ways. A query that works in H2 fails in production because H2 supports syntax that your production database doesn't, or handles NULLs differently, or has different collation rules.

Testcontainers launches a real database in a Docker container during the test. Your JPA queries run against the actual database engine you deploy to production — same SQL dialect, same type system, same edge cases. The setup takes a few seconds for container startup, but the queries execute against truth, not approximation.

The critical annotation: **`@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)`** tells Spring Boot NOT to replace your DataSource with an embedded database. Without it, `@DataJpaTest` ignores your `application-test.yml` DataSource configuration and uses H2 regardless of what you've configured.

The investment pays off when a production bug traces back to a query that worked in H2 but fails in PostgreSQL. Common examples: H2 accepts `GROUP BY 1` (positional reference) while some MySQL modes reject it. H2's `CONCAT` handles NULL differently than PostgreSQL. H2's `LIMIT/OFFSET` syntax works, but pagination edge cases with custom sorting behave differently. Testing against the real database catches these before production.

sections.title: MockMvc Tests the Controller Layer Without Starting a Server — That's Both Its Power and Its Limitation
sections.content:
MockMvc simulates HTTP requests through Spring's `DispatcherServlet` without starting a real HTTP server. No socket binding, no TCP overhead — requests go directly through the servlet pipeline. This makes controller tests fast (milliseconds) while still exercising the full Spring MVC stack: request mapping, parameter binding, validation, exception handling, and content negotiation.

The limitation: MockMvc bypasses the HTTP transport layer. Issues that only appear with a real server — CORS configuration, SSL, response compression, multipart parsing edge cases — won't be caught. For these, you need `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` with `TestRestTemplate`.

MockMvc pairs best with `@WebMvcTest`, which loads only the controller layer. Dependencies like services and repositories are mocked with `@MockBean`. This combination tests that your controller correctly maps requests, validates input, calls the right service method, and returns the right HTTP status and response body — without touching the database or any real service.

The key advantage of MockMvc over a real HTTP test: **speed and determinism.** No port binding, no network stack, no race conditions from async startup. A MockMvc test suite with 50 controller tests runs in under 5 seconds because the servlet simulation has zero network overhead. This makes it practical to test every request mapping, every validation rule, and every error response without slowing down the developer feedback loop.

sections.title: Choosing the Wrong Test Annotation Adds 10 Seconds Per Test Class — Here's the Decision Tree
sections.content:
Spring Boot provides test annotations that range from loading nothing (`@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`) to loading everything (`@SpringBootTest`). Choosing the right one is the single biggest factor in test suite speed.

The decision tree is simple. Ask: **what am I testing?**

- **Business logic in a service?** → No Spring needed. `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` + `@Mock` + `@InjectMocks`. Runs in milliseconds.
- **Controller request/response mapping?** → `@WebMvcTest(Controller.class)`. Loads web layer only. Runs in ~2 seconds.
- **JPA repository query?** → `@DataJpaTest`. Loads JPA layer with H2 or Testcontainers. Runs in ~3 seconds.
- **JSON serialization?** → `@JsonTest`. Loads Jackson only.
- **REST client behavior?** → `@RestClientTest`. Loads RestTemplate/WebClient with a mock server.
- **Cross-cutting integration?** → `@SpringBootTest`. Full context. 10-30 seconds.

The pattern: **start with the narrowest annotation and widen only if the test requires more context.** If you find yourself adding `@MockBean` for half the beans in a `@SpringBootTest`, you probably need a narrower slice.

sections.title: Test Annotation Decision Matrix
sections.content:
| What you're testing | Annotation | Context size | Startup time | Mock style |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Service business logic | `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension)` | None | <100ms | `@Mock` |
| Controller mapping + validation | `@WebMvcTest` | Web layer | ~2s | `@MockBean` |
| JPA query correctness | `@DataJpaTest` | JPA layer | ~3s | None (real DB) |
| JSON serialization | `@JsonTest` | Jackson only | ~1s | None |
| REST client | `@RestClientTest` | RestTemplate | ~2s | `MockRestServiceServer` |
| Full app integration | `@SpringBootTest` | Everything | 10-30s | `@MockBean` |
| Security rules | `@WebMvcTest` + `@WithMockUser` | Web + Security | ~2s | `@MockBean` |

The startup time column is the hidden cost. 50 test classes using `@SpringBootTest` add 8-25 minutes to CI. The same tests using slices add 2-3 minutes.

sections.title: Context Caching — Why Mock Combinations Matter More Than Test Count
sections.content:
Spring caches the application context and reuses it across test classes with the same configuration. A `@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)` with `@MockBean UserService` creates one context. A second test class with the same annotation and same `@MockBean` reuses the cached context — zero startup cost.

The cache invalidation happens when the configuration changes: different `@MockBean` sets, different `@TestPropertySource` values, different active profiles. Each unique combination creates a new cache entry and triggers a new context startup.

The practical impact: 10 `@WebMvcTest` classes with the same `@MockBean` service boot ONE context. 10 classes where each mocks a different set of beans boot 10 separate contexts. Standardizing which beans you mock across test classes — using the same base class or consistent mock sets — is the most effective way to speed up a test suite.

Use `--debug` in Surefire/Failsafe to log context cache hits and misses. If you see mostly misses, audit your mock combinations.

sections.title: Real-World Test Suite Structure — How the Pyramid Looks in Code
sections.content:
A well-structured Spring Boot test suite follows a clear directory pattern that mirrors the testing pyramid.

```
src/test/java/com/app/
  unit/           ← @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) — 80% of tests
    service/
    mapper/
    validator/
  integration/    ← @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest — 15% of tests
    controller/
    repository/
  e2e/            ← @SpringBootTest(RANDOM_PORT) — 5% of tests
    smoke/
    security/
```

The directory structure communicates intent: anything in `unit/` should run without Spring, anything in `integration/` needs a test slice, and `e2e/` needs the full context.

Configure Surefire and Failsafe to run these in stages: unit tests in `mvn test` (Surefire), integration and E2E tests in `mvn verify` (Failsafe). Developers run `mvn test` locally for fast feedback (~30 seconds). CI runs `mvn verify` for full confidence (~3-5 minutes). This separation prevents slow integration tests from blocking the developer's commit cycle.

The 80/15/5 ratio is a guideline, not a rule. Some domains (CRUD apps with little logic) naturally have more integration tests. Complex domains (financial calculations, rule engines) have more unit tests. The ratio should reflect where the complexity lives.

The nuance is context caching. Spring reuses cached contexts across test classes with identical configurations. Different `@MockBean` combinations create different cache keys, triggering new context startups. Standardizing mock combinations across test classes is the easiest way to speed up a large test suite.

Start with the narrowest annotation and widen only if the test fails to run without more context.

sections.title: A New Container Per Test Class Turns a 3-Second Startup Into a 3-Minute Suite
sections.content:
Testcontainers launches real infrastructure (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, Elasticsearch) in Docker containers during tests. The setup is straightforward: declare a container, start it, inject the connection URL, run your tests. The complexity is in **lifecycle management** — specifically, when containers start and stop.

The default pattern (`@Container` on a non-static field) starts a new container for every test method. A static `@Container` starts once per test class. But a test suite with 20 `@DataJpaTest` classes, each starting its own PostgreSQL container, spends 60 seconds just on container startups — the actual tests might take 10 seconds.

The solution is **shared containers across test classes.** Define the container in a base class (or use Testcontainers' reuse feature), start it once for the entire suite, and reuse the same container across all test classes. The container starts in ~3 seconds, the suite runs in ~15 seconds instead of ~75 seconds.

One subtlety: `@DataJpaTest` rolls back transactions by default, so test isolation is automatic. For containers without transaction support (Redis, Elasticsearch), you need explicit cleanup between tests — `@BeforeEach` with a `flushAll()` or `deleteAll()`.

The container reuse feature (`testcontainers.reuse.enable=true`) is particularly valuable during development. Without reuse, every `mvn test` invocation starts fresh containers. With reuse, the containers persist between runs — your second test run starts instantly. In CI, reuse is typically disabled because each build should start clean. This dual mode (reuse locally, fresh in CI) gives the best of both worlds: fast developer iteration and clean CI verification.

sections.title: The Shared Container Pattern — One Container for All Tests
Best Practices That Prevent Flaky Tests and Slow Suites
sections.content:
**Pin container image versions.** `new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:15.4")` not `"postgres:latest"`. Latest changes without warning, introducing test failures from image updates, not code changes.

**Use `@DynamicPropertySource` over hardcoded ports.** Testcontainers assigns random ports to avoid conflicts. Hardcoding `jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/test` fails when another test or service uses port 5432.

**Pre-pull images in CI.** Container startup includes image download time on first run. Add a CI step that pulls images before running tests: `docker pull postgres:15.4`. This moves the download time out of the test execution.

**Limit container resource usage.** In CI environments with limited resources, set memory limits: `.withCreateContainerCmdModifier(cmd -> cmd.getHostConfig().withMemory(512 * 1024 * 1024))`. A runaway container consuming all CI memory causes all tests to fail.

**Test data isolation matters.** `@DataJpaTest` rolls back transactions automatically. For Redis tests, call `redisTemplate.getConnectionFactory().getConnection().flushAll()` in `@BeforeEach`. For Elasticsearch, delete and recreate the index. Without cleanup, tests pass individually but fail when run together.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Testcontainers runs real infrastructure in Docker — PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka — during tests. The biggest mistake is starting a new container per test class. A 3-second container startup multiplied by 20 test classes adds a minute of pure overhead.

The fix: shared containers. Define a static container in a base class, start it once for the entire suite, and reuse it. With `withReuse(true)` and `testcontainers.reuse.enable=true`, the container even survives between test runs during development.

Always pin image versions — `postgres:15.4` not `postgres:latest`. Use `@DynamicPropertySource` for connection URLs because Testcontainers assigns random ports. And handle test isolation explicitly: `@DataJpaTest` rolls back transactions automatically, but Redis and Elasticsearch need manual cleanup between tests.

Pre-pull images in CI to avoid download time during test execution.

sections.content:
- **Starting a new container per test class multiplies startup time** — 20 classes with individual PostgreSQL containers = 60 seconds of startup; a shared static container in a base class starts once in 3 seconds.
- **`withReuse(true)` keeps containers running between test executions** — requires `testcontainers.reuse.enable=true` in `~/.testcontainers.properties`; eliminates startup time during iterative development.
- **Pin image versions: `postgres:15.4` not `postgres:latest`** — `latest` changes without warning; test failures from image updates, not code changes, are impossible to diagnose quickly.
- **`@DynamicPropertySource` handles random port assignment** — Testcontainers assigns random ports to avoid conflicts; hardcoded ports fail in CI where other services may use the same port.
- **`@DataJpaTest` rolls back transactions; Redis/Elasticsearch need explicit cleanup** — without `flushAll()` or index recreation in `@BeforeEach`, tests pass individually but fail in suite order.

For @Async Spring methods, either use CountDownLatch/CompletableFuture to wait, or test the underlying method directly without the async wrapper in unit tests. sections.title: Thread.sleep() in Async Tests Is a Bug, Not a Strategy
sections.content:
Testing asynchronous code requires synchronization between the test thread and the async execution. The naive approach — `Thread.sleep(2000)` — is both slow (always waits the full duration) and flaky (fails when execution takes longer than expected on a loaded CI server).

`CompletableFuture` testing is simpler than it appears because the future itself provides the synchronization point. Call `.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` or `.join()` with a timeout — the test blocks until the result is available or times out.

The harder case is testing `@Async` methods in Spring, where the method returns before the async work completes. Here you need an explicit synchronization mechanism: `CountDownLatch`, `Awaitility`, or a `CompletableFuture` that the async code completes. The test waits on this mechanism with a timeout, proceeding as soon as the async work finishes.

The key principle: **every async test needs an explicit synchronization point.** For `CompletableFuture`, the future itself is the synchronization. For `@Async void` methods, you create one — typically by observing a side effect (database write, event, flag). The test waits on this synchronization point with a timeout, never on a fixed sleep duration. Awaitility provides this pattern out of the box with `await().atMost().untilAsserted()`, polling the assertion until it passes or the timeout expires.

sections.title: Testing CompletableFuture — The Future IS the Synchronization
Testing @Async Methods — When the Method Returns void
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
For `CompletableFuture`, the future itself is your synchronization point — call `.get(5, SECONDS)` and assert on the result. No `Thread.sleep()` needed. For failures, `future.get()` wraps the exception in `ExecutionException`, so assert on the cause.

The harder case is `@Async void` methods. There's no future to wait on, so you need to observe a side effect. **Awaitility** is the standard tool: `await().atMost(10, SECONDS).untilAsserted(() -> assertThat(...))`. It polls the assertion until it passes or times out — adapting to actual execution speed instead of sleeping for an arbitrary duration.

`Thread.sleep()` is always wrong in tests. It's too slow (always waits the full duration) and too flaky (fails when CI is loaded). Every async test should use either the future's `.get()` or Awaitility.

Remember: `@Async` requires Spring's proxy, so these tests need `@SpringBootTest` with `@EnableAsync`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Thread.sleep()` is always wrong in async tests** — too slow (always waits full duration) and too flaky (fails on loaded CI); use `future.get(timeout)` or Awaitility instead.
- **`CompletableFuture.get()` IS the synchronization point** — blocks until result is available; JUnit 5's `assertTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5), () -> future.get())` provides clear failure messages.
- **`await().atMost().untilAsserted()` polls until the assertion passes** — adapts to actual execution speed; fast locally, tolerant of CI slowness; standard for testing `@Async void` methods.
- **`@Async` methods need `@SpringBootTest` + `@EnableAsync`** — the async proxy is created by Spring's post-processor; without a Spring context, the method runs synchronously and the test passes for the wrong reason.
- **`future.get()` wraps exceptions in `ExecutionException`** — use `.hasCauseInstanceOf()` to assert on the actual exception; direct `assertThrows(UserNotFoundException.class)` won't match.

sections.title: Disabling Security in Tests Means You're Not Testing Security — Use @WithMockUser Instead
sections.content:
The instinct when security makes tests fail is to disable it: `@WebMvcTest(excludeAutoConfiguration = SecurityAutoConfiguration.class)`. This makes the tests pass — and completely removes the value of testing that authorized users can access endpoints and unauthorized users cannot.

Spring Security Test provides annotations that create mock authentication without requiring actual login flows. `@WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN")` creates an authenticated user with the ADMIN role. `@WithAnonymousUser` creates an unauthenticated request. These work with both `@WebMvcTest` and `@SpringBootTest` because they inject authentication into Spring Security's context before the request is processed.

The correct approach: **test both the allowed and denied paths.** A security test that only verifies "admin can access" without verifying "user cannot access" proves nothing. The value is in confirming that your security rules accept what they should and reject what they should — testing one side without the other is incomplete.

Spring Security's test support goes beyond simple role checks. `@WithMockUser` handles basic authentication. `@WithSecurityContext` builds custom authentication objects for JWT, OAuth2, or LDAP-based security. `SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.jwt()` creates mock JWT tokens with specific claims and authorities — useful when your security rules depend on JWT claims like `scope`, `tenant_id`, or custom attributes rather than simple roles.

sections.title: Testing Role-Based Access With @WithMockUser
Testing Method-Level Security — @PreAuthorize and @Secured
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Don't disable security in tests — use `@WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN")` to create mock authentication. The test should verify **both paths**: that authorized users can access the endpoint AND that unauthorized users are rejected. A security test that only checks the allowed path proves nothing.

For controller security, `@WebMvcTest` with `@WithMockUser` works because Spring Security auto-configuration is included in the web slice. For method-level `@PreAuthorize` security, you need `@SpringBootTest` because the security proxy is created by Spring AOP.

The critical thing to test is the **denied path.** A misconfigured `@PreAuthorize` silently allows everything. If `assertThrows(AccessDeniedException.class)` doesn't throw, the security rule isn't active — and the "allowed" test would still pass, hiding the bug.

For JWT or custom authentication, use `@WithSecurityContext` to build a custom security context with your principal and claims.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Disabling security in tests means you're not testing security** — `excludeAutoConfiguration = SecurityAutoConfiguration.class` makes tests pass but removes all authorization verification; use `@WithMockUser` instead.
- **Test both allowed AND denied paths** — a security test that only verifies "admin can access" without verifying "user cannot access" catches nothing; the denied path is the important one.
- **`@WebMvcTest` includes Spring Security auto-configuration** — no need for `@SpringBootTest` to test controller-level security; `@WithMockUser` injects authentication before the request.
- **Method-level `@PreAuthorize` needs `@SpringBootTest`** — the security proxy is created by Spring AOP; without a context, `@PreAuthorize` is ignored and the method executes without authorization checks.
- **`@WithSecurityContext` builds custom authentication** — for JWT-based security with custom claims, define a factory that populates the `SecurityContext` with your principal and authorities.

sections.title: 10 Copy-Pasted Test Methods for 10 Inputs Is a Maintenance Nightmare — Parameterize It
sections.content:
When you need to test the same logic with different inputs, the naive approach is copying the test method 10 times and changing the input value. This creates 10 nearly identical methods that must all be updated when the logic changes. `@ParameterizedTest` runs the same test method with different inputs, replacing 10 methods with one.

JUnit 5 provides multiple sources for parameters: `@ValueSource` for single-type primitives, `@CsvSource` for multi-column data, `@EnumSource` for enum values, and `@MethodSource` for complex objects. Each source feeds rows of data into the test method, and JUnit reports each row as a separate test case with a descriptive name.

The real power isn't reducing line count — it's **revealing patterns.** When you see all inputs and expected outputs together, edge cases become visible. Adding a new test case is one line, not copying an entire method. And when the assertion logic changes, you change it in one place.

Beyond reducing code duplication, parameterized tests improve **test documentation.** When all valid and invalid inputs are listed in one place, the test becomes a specification of the method's behavior. A new developer reads the `@CsvSource` or `@MethodSource` and immediately understands all the cases the method handles. Adding a new edge case is one line, not a new method with setup, act, and assert boilerplate. JUnit 5 reports each parameter set as a separate test case, so failures pinpoint the exact failing input without extra debugging.

sections.title: @ValueSource, @CsvSource, and @MethodSource — When to Use Each
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@ParameterizedTest` runs the same test with different inputs — replacing 10 copy-pasted methods with one. JUnit 5 reports each input as a separate test case, so you still see exactly which combination failed.

Three sources cover most cases. `@ValueSource` for single primitives — testing validation against blank strings, negative numbers. `@CsvSource` for input-output pairs — price and discount percentage mapped to expected result. `@MethodSource` for complex objects — returning `Stream<Arguments>` with custom types.

The real value isn't less code — it's **revealing edge cases.** When all inputs and expected outputs are listed together, gaps become obvious. Adding a new test case is one line instead of copying a method.

`@MethodSource` methods must be `static` and return `Stream<Arguments>`. Use descriptive names — they appear in test reports, and a failed parameterized test must immediately show which combination failed.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@ValueSource` for single primitives, `@CsvSource` for multi-column, `@MethodSource` for complex objects** — each source feeds data into the same test method; JUnit reports each row as a separate test case.
- **`@MethodSource` methods must be `static` and return `Stream<Arguments>`** — non-static methods cause `PreconditionViolationException`; the method name must match the string in `@MethodSource` or default to the test method name.
- **Custom display names: `@ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} with {1}%")`** — default displays show raw arguments; custom names give readable test reports where failures immediately identify the failing input.
- **Edge cases become visible when inputs are listed together** — seeing all boundary values in one place reveals gaps (null, empty, negative, zero, max) that separate methods hide.
- **`@EnumSource` tests all enum values automatically** — `@EnumSource(Status.class)` passes each enum constant; `@EnumSource(mode = EXCLUDE, names = "DELETED")` skips specific values; ensures new enum values are tested without updating test code.

sections.title: Kafka Tests Need a Real Broker — @EmbeddedKafka Gives You One Without Docker
sections.content:
Testing Kafka consumers and producers requires a broker. Mocking `KafkaTemplate` tests serialization but misses the actual consume-produce lifecycle — partition assignment, offset management, consumer group coordination. `@EmbeddedKafka` starts an in-memory Kafka broker as part of the Spring test context. No Docker, no external infrastructure.

The embedded broker handles topic creation, partition assignment, and offset tracking exactly like a real broker. Messages sent by `KafkaTemplate` are stored in the embedded broker's log, and `@KafkaListener` instances consume them through the normal consumer group protocol.

The biggest testing mistake is `Thread.sleep()` for synchronization. Kafka consumption is asynchronous — the listener processes messages in a background thread. `Awaitility` or `CountDownLatch` provides proper synchronization that adapts to actual processing speed. A 5-second sleep that "works" locally fails on a loaded CI server where the consumer takes 6 seconds to start.

For teams running many Kafka tests, the embedded broker's startup cost matters. Like Testcontainers, use a shared embedded broker across test classes. Define the `@EmbeddedKafka` configuration in a base class or custom annotation, and Spring's context caching reuses the same broker instance. Different topic configurations invalidate the cache, so standardize topics across test classes where possible.

sections.title: The Full Pattern — Produce, Consume, Assert With Awaitility
Common Pitfalls — Consumer Group Conflicts and Topic Reuse
sections.content:
**Use unique consumer group IDs per test class.** If two test classes share a consumer group ID and run in the same JVM, they compete for partitions. Use `groupId = "test-" + UUID.randomUUID()` or class-specific group IDs.

**Clean up between tests.** The embedded broker persists messages between test methods. If test A sends a message and test B reads from the same topic, test B might see test A's message. Use unique topics per test or clear the consumer's position with `seekToEnd()`.

**Verify error handling, not just happy path.** The highest-value Kafka tests verify that malformed messages reach the DLT, that retries exhaust correctly, and that the consumer continues processing after a failure. These tests catch configuration regressions — someone changes the error handler and the test detects that DLT routing silently broke.

For teams using Testcontainers instead of `@EmbeddedKafka`, the trade-off is startup time vs fidelity. The embedded broker is faster (in-memory) but doesn't support all Kafka features (transactions require specific configuration). Testcontainers' Kafka module runs a real Confluent/Apache Kafka image but adds container startup time.

Another common issue: **serialization configuration in tests must match production.** If your production `KafkaTemplate` uses `JsonSerializer` with specific type mappings, the test template must use the same configuration. A test that sends raw strings but the consumer expects JSON-serialized objects fails with deserialization errors that don't reflect real behavior.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@EmbeddedKafka` starts an in-memory Kafka broker — no Docker needed. The test produces a message, the `@KafkaListener` consumes it asynchronously, and you verify the side effect with Awaitility: `await().atMost(10, SECONDS).untilAsserted(() -> ...)`.

Set `partitions = 1` for deterministic tests — multiple partitions introduce non-deterministic assignment. Use unique consumer group IDs per test class to avoid partition competition.

The highest-value tests verify error handling: send malformed data, verify it reaches the DLT with `KafkaTestUtils.getSingleRecord()`. These tests catch configuration regressions when someone changes the error handler and DLT routing silently breaks.

Never use `Thread.sleep()` — it's slow and flaky. Awaitility adapts to actual processing speed, making tests fast locally and tolerant of CI slowness.

Use unique consumer group IDs per test class to prevent partition competition, and set `partitions = 1` for deterministic ordering in assertions.

questions.question: What is Test-Driven Development (TDD) and how does the red-green-refactor cycle work in practice?
questions.title: Test-Driven Development: Red-Green-Refactor Cycle
questions.direct_answer: TDD is a development practice where you write a failing test before writing the production code. The cycle is: Red — write the smallest possible failing test. Green — write the minimum production code to make it pass. Refactor — clean up the code while keeping all tests green. Benefits include built-in test coverage, emergent design, and a safety net for future changes. The key discipline is writing the minimal code to pass each test, then improving it in the refactor phase.

sections.title: TDD Isn't About Testing — It's About Designing Code Through Usage Before Implementation
sections.content:
Test-Driven Development means writing the test **before** the production code. The cycle is red-green-refactor: write a failing test (red), write the minimum code to make it pass (green), then improve the code without changing behavior (refactor).

The common misconception is that TDD is a testing technique. It's actually a **design technique.** By writing the test first, you're forced to think about the public API before the implementation — what arguments does the method take? What does it return? What exceptions does it throw? The test becomes a specification of behavior, and the code is written to satisfy that specification.

The biggest mistake is writing the full implementation first and calling it TDD because tests exist. TDD's value comes from the **sequence**: the test drives the design. When you write the implementation first, the test validates what you already built — it doesn't shape the API or catch design problems early.

TDD works best for **business logic and domain code** — services, validators, calculators, state machines. It's less useful for wiring code (controllers, configuration) where the design is dictated by frameworks. Don't force TDD on code where the test would just verify that you called Spring's API correctly.

sections.title: Red-Green-Refactor — A Concrete Walk-Through
When TDD Helps vs When It Gets in the Way
sections.content:
**TDD works best for:**
- Business logic with clear inputs and outputs (calculators, validators, transformers)
- Domain models with state transitions (order lifecycle, approval workflows)
- Algorithms with known edge cases (parsing, formatting, search)
- Bug fixes — write a test that reproduces the bug first, then fix it; the test prevents regression

**TDD is less useful for:**
- CRUD controllers where the design is dictated by the framework
- Configuration classes where the test would just verify Spring wiring
- UI code where behavior depends on visual rendering
- Exploratory prototyping where the API is still being discovered

The practical compromise: use TDD for domain logic and service layers. Write tests after for controllers, repositories, and integration points. The goal is confident, well-designed code — not dogmatic adherence to a process. A team that writes excellent tests after implementation is better off than a team that writes poor tests before it.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
TDD is red-green-refactor: write a failing test first, write the minimum code to pass it, then refactor with the test as a safety net. The cycle repeats — each test adds one behavior, and the implementation grows incrementally.

The misconception is that TDD is about testing. It's actually a **design technique.** By writing the test first, you design the API before the implementation — what the method takes, what it returns, what it throws. The test is a specification.

TDD works best for business logic with clear inputs and outputs — calculators, validators, state machines. It's less useful for framework-driven code like controllers and configuration, where the design is dictated by Spring, not by your domain.

For bug fixes, TDD is invaluable: write a test that reproduces the bug, verify it fails, fix it, verify it passes. The test prevents regression permanently.

sections.content:
- **Red-green-refactor: test first, then implement, then improve** — the sequence matters; writing the test first forces API design decisions before implementation; writing tests after validates what you built but doesn't shape the design.
- **TDD is a design technique, not a testing technique** — the test specifies behavior before code exists; method signatures, parameter types, and return values are decided by writing the test first.
- **Best for business logic, not framework wiring** — calculators, validators, state machines benefit most; controllers and configuration where the design is dictated by Spring gain little from test-first approach.
- **Bug fix TDD: reproduce the bug as a test first** — verify the test fails, fix the code, verify it passes; the test prevents regression permanently; this is the highest-ROI TDD application.
- **"Minimum code to make it pass" prevents over-engineering** — each test adds one requirement; the implementation grows incrementally; premature abstractions are avoided because they aren't needed to pass the current test.

sections.title: Mockito Gives You Three Capabilities — Stubbing, Verification, and Argument Capture
sections.content:
Most developers learn `when().thenReturn()` and stop. But Mockito has three distinct capabilities that serve different testing needs, and using the wrong one weakens your tests.

**Stubbing** (`when().thenReturn()`) controls what the mock returns. This is input to the code under test — you set up the world the code will see.

**Verification** (`verify()`) confirms the code under test called a dependency with expected arguments. This is output validation — did the service actually call the repository's `save()` method? Did it call the notification client?

**Argument capture** (`ArgumentCaptor`) grabs the actual object passed to a mock method so you can assert on its fields. This bridges the gap between stubbing (what goes in) and verification (what comes out) — it tells you *exactly what was passed* to a dependency.

The distinction matters because each serves a different testing purpose. Stubbing sets up preconditions. Verification confirms side effects. Argument capture validates the data flow between components. A well-written unit test often uses all three: stub the repository to return test data, verify the email service was called, and capture the email to assert it has the right subject and recipient.

sections.title: verify() — Testing Interactions, Not Just Return Values
ArgumentCaptor — When verify() Isn't Enough
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@Mock` creates stubs that return defaults. `@Spy` wraps real objects — real methods execute unless overridden with `doReturn().when()`. The key mistake is using `when().thenReturn()` with spies, which calls the real method before stubbing.

`verify()` confirms interactions — did the service call `save()`? Did it send the notification? `verify(mock, never())` is equally important for testing that error paths don't trigger side effects.

`ArgumentCaptor` captures arguments passed to mocks for detailed assertions. When `verify()` tells you the method was called, the captor tells you *what was passed*. This is essential for testing services that transform data between layers — asserting that the request DTO was correctly mapped to the domain object.

My pattern: stub the inputs, call the method, verify the interactions, capture arguments for important assertions.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`doReturn().when()` for spies, `when().thenReturn()` for mocks** — with spies, `when().thenReturn()` executes the real method before stubbing, causing side effects; `doReturn().when()` avoids this.
- **`verify(mock, never())` tests negative paths** — confirming that error handling does NOT send notifications or save data is as important as confirming the happy path does.
- **`ArgumentCaptor.getValue()` inspects passed arguments** — replaces `any()` in verify; captures the actual object for field-level assertions; essential for testing data transformation between layers.
- **`verifyNoMoreInteractions()` makes tests brittle** — couples tests to implementation details; prefer verifying specific important interactions over asserting nothing else happened.
- **`thenAnswer()` for dynamic return values** — `when(repo.save(any())).thenAnswer(inv -> inv.getArgument(0))` returns the saved object with modifications; more flexible than `thenReturn()` for testing persistence logic.

sections.title: @SpringBootTest Loads Everything — That's Why It's Slow and Why Slices Exist
sections.content:
`@SpringBootTest` starts the full Spring application context — every bean, every auto-configuration, every component scan. This gives maximum fidelity but at a cost: context startup takes 5-30 seconds depending on the application. For a project with 200 tests all using `@SpringBootTest`, the test suite runs for 30+ minutes.

**Test slices** load only the parts of the context relevant to what you're testing. `@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)` loads the web layer — controller, filters, converters — but not services, repositories, or database connections. `@DataJpaTest` loads JPA repositories and an embedded H2 database but not controllers or services.

The performance difference is dramatic. A `@WebMvcTest` starts in under 2 seconds. The same test with `@SpringBootTest` takes 10-15 seconds because it loads the entire application including database connections, message brokers, and scheduled tasks that the test doesn't need.

Spring caches application contexts across tests with the same configuration — but slices with different `@MockBean` annotations create different cache keys, triggering new context creation. Minimizing distinct `@MockBean` combinations across test classes keeps context caching effective.

sections.title: Test Slice Selection — What Each Annotation Loads
sections.content:
| Annotation | What it loads | What it excludes | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@SpringBootTest` | Everything | Nothing | Full integration tests, app startup verification |
| `@WebMvcTest` | Controllers, filters, `@ControllerAdvice` | Services, repositories, DB | Controller request/response testing |
| `@DataJpaTest` | JPA repos, `EntityManager`, H2/Testcontainers | Controllers, services | Repository query verification |
| `@WebFluxTest` | WebFlux controllers | Everything else | Reactive controller testing |
| `@JsonTest` | Jackson `ObjectMapper` | Everything else | JSON serialization/deserialization |
| `@RestClientTest` | `RestTemplate` / `WebClient` with mock server | Everything else | External API client testing |

The pattern: **use the narrowest slice that covers what you're testing.** If you're testing a controller's request mapping and validation, `@WebMvcTest` is faster and more focused than `@SpringBootTest`. If you're testing a JPA query, `@DataJpaTest` loads only what the repository needs.

sections.title: When @SpringBootTest Is Actually the Right Choice
Test Profile and Property Overrides — Isolating Test Configuration
sections.content:
Test slices often need different configuration than production. `@TestPropertySource(properties = "spring.jpa.show-sql=true")` overrides individual properties. `@ActiveProfiles("test")` activates a test-specific `application-test.yml` with test database URLs, disabled scheduling, and mock external service endpoints.

The hierarchy matters: `@TestPropertySource` overrides profile properties, which override `application.yml`. This lets you keep most configuration in the default file and override only what's test-specific.

One pattern that prevents test configuration drift: create a `src/test/resources/application-test.yml` that disables everything tests don't need — scheduled tasks (`spring.task.scheduling.enabled=false`), actuator endpoints, and Kafka auto-configuration. Tests start faster because Spring skips auto-configuration for components that aren't part of the test.

For `@DataJpaTest`, properties like `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop` ensure a clean schema per test run. Combined with `@Transactional` rollback, this gives complete test isolation without manual cleanup scripts.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@SpringBootTest` loads the full application context — every bean, every auto-configuration. It gives maximum fidelity but takes 10-30 seconds to start. Test slices like `@WebMvcTest` and `@DataJpaTest` load only the relevant portion, starting in under 2 seconds.

`@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)` loads just the controller layer — no services, no repositories, no database. You mock dependencies with `@MockBean`. `@DataJpaTest` loads JPA repositories with an embedded database — no controllers.

The rule: **use the narrowest slice that covers what you're testing.** Reserve `@SpringBootTest` for smoke tests and cross-cutting integration tests — maybe 10-20% of your suite. The rest should use slices.

One thing that trips people up: Spring caches contexts, but each unique `@MockBean` combination creates a new cache key. Minimizing distinct mock combinations across test classes keeps caching effective and the suite fast.

sections.title: A New Container Per Test Class Turns a 3-Second Startup Into a 3-Minute Suite
sections.content:
Testcontainers launches real infrastructure (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, Elasticsearch) in Docker containers during tests. The setup is straightforward: declare a container, start it, inject the connection URL, run your tests. The complexity is in **lifecycle management** — specifically, when containers start and stop.

The default pattern (`@Container` on a non-static field) starts a new container for every test method. A static `@Container` starts once per test class. But a test suite with 20 `@DataJpaTest` classes, each starting its own PostgreSQL container, spends 60 seconds just on container startups — the actual tests might take 10 seconds.

The solution is **shared containers across test classes.** Define the container in a base class (or use Testcontainers' reuse feature), start it once for the entire suite, and reuse the same container across all test classes. The container starts in ~3 seconds, the suite runs in ~15 seconds instead of ~75 seconds.

One subtlety: `@DataJpaTest` rolls back transactions by default, so test isolation is automatic. For containers without transaction support (Redis, Elasticsearch), you need explicit cleanup between tests — `@BeforeEach` with a `flushAll()` or `deleteAll()`.

The container reuse feature (`testcontainers.reuse.enable=true`) is particularly valuable during development. Without reuse, every `mvn test` invocation starts fresh containers. With reuse, the containers persist between runs — your second test run starts instantly. In CI, reuse is typically disabled because each build should start clean. This dual mode (reuse locally, fresh in CI) gives the best of both worlds: fast developer iteration and clean CI verification.

sections.title: The Shared Container Pattern — One Container for All Tests
Best Practices That Prevent Flaky Tests and Slow Suites
sections.content:
**Pin container image versions.** `new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:15.4")` not `"postgres:latest"`. Latest changes without warning, introducing test failures from image updates, not code changes.

**Use `@DynamicPropertySource` over hardcoded ports.** Testcontainers assigns random ports to avoid conflicts. Hardcoding `jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/test` fails when another test or service uses port 5432.

**Pre-pull images in CI.** Container startup includes image download time on first run. Add a CI step that pulls images before running tests: `docker pull postgres:15.4`. This moves the download time out of the test execution.

**Limit container resource usage.** In CI environments with limited resources, set memory limits: `.withCreateContainerCmdModifier(cmd -> cmd.getHostConfig().withMemory(512 * 1024 * 1024))`. A runaway container consuming all CI memory causes all tests to fail.

**Test data isolation matters.** `@DataJpaTest` rolls back transactions automatically. For Redis tests, call `redisTemplate.getConnectionFactory().getConnection().flushAll()` in `@BeforeEach`. For Elasticsearch, delete and recreate the index. Without cleanup, tests pass individually but fail when run together.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Testcontainers runs real infrastructure in Docker — PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka — during tests. The biggest mistake is starting a new container per test class. A 3-second container startup multiplied by 20 test classes adds a minute of pure overhead.

The fix: shared containers. Define a static container in a base class, start it once for the entire suite, and reuse it. With `withReuse(true)` and `testcontainers.reuse.enable=true`, the container even survives between test runs during development.

Always pin image versions — `postgres:15.4` not `postgres:latest`. Use `@DynamicPropertySource` for connection URLs because Testcontainers assigns random ports. And handle test isolation explicitly: `@DataJpaTest` rolls back transactions automatically, but Redis and Elasticsearch need manual cleanup between tests.

Pre-pull images in CI to avoid download time during test execution.

sections.title: MockMvc Tests the Controller Layer Without Starting a Server — That's Both Its Power and Its Limitation
sections.content:
MockMvc simulates HTTP requests through Spring's `DispatcherServlet` without starting a real HTTP server. No socket binding, no TCP overhead — requests go directly through the servlet pipeline. This makes controller tests fast (milliseconds) while still exercising the full Spring MVC stack: request mapping, parameter binding, validation, exception handling, and content negotiation.

The limitation: MockMvc bypasses the HTTP transport layer. Issues that only appear with a real server — CORS configuration, SSL, response compression, multipart parsing edge cases — won't be caught. For these, you need `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` with `TestRestTemplate`.

MockMvc pairs best with `@WebMvcTest`, which loads only the controller layer. Dependencies like services and repositories are mocked with `@MockBean`. This combination tests that your controller correctly maps requests, validates input, calls the right service method, and returns the right HTTP status and response body — without touching the database or any real service.

The key advantage of MockMvc over a real HTTP test: **speed and determinism.** No port binding, no network stack, no race conditions from async startup. A MockMvc test suite with 50 controller tests runs in under 5 seconds because the servlet simulation has zero network overhead. This makes it practical to test every request mapping, every validation rule, and every error response without slowing down the developer feedback loop.

sections.title: TDD Isn't About Testing — It's About Designing Code Through Usage Before Implementation
sections.content:
Test-Driven Development means writing the test **before** the production code. The cycle is red-green-refactor: write a failing test (red), write the minimum code to make it pass (green), then improve the code without changing behavior (refactor).

The common misconception is that TDD is a testing technique. It's actually a **design technique.** By writing the test first, you're forced to think about the public API before the implementation — what arguments does the method take? What does it return? What exceptions does it throw? The test becomes a specification of behavior, and the code is written to satisfy that specification.

The biggest mistake is writing the full implementation first and calling it TDD because tests exist. TDD's value comes from the **sequence**: the test drives the design. When you write the implementation first, the test validates what you already built — it doesn't shape the API or catch design problems early.

TDD works best for **business logic and domain code** — services, validators, calculators, state machines. It's less useful for wiring code (controllers, configuration) where the design is dictated by frameworks. Don't force TDD on code where the test would just verify that you called Spring's API correctly.

sections.title: Red-Green-Refactor — A Concrete Walk-Through
When TDD Helps vs When It Gets in the Way
sections.content:
**TDD works best for:**
- Business logic with clear inputs and outputs (calculators, validators, transformers)
- Domain models with state transitions (order lifecycle, approval workflows)
- Algorithms with known edge cases (parsing, formatting, search)
- Bug fixes — write a test that reproduces the bug first, then fix it; the test prevents regression

**TDD is less useful for:**
- CRUD controllers where the design is dictated by the framework
- Configuration classes where the test would just verify Spring wiring
- UI code where behavior depends on visual rendering
- Exploratory prototyping where the API is still being discovered

The practical compromise: use TDD for domain logic and service layers. Write tests after for controllers, repositories, and integration points. The goal is confident, well-designed code — not dogmatic adherence to a process. A team that writes excellent tests after implementation is better off than a team that writes poor tests before it.

sections.title: assertEquals Tells You It Failed — AssertJ Tells You Why
sections.content:
JUnit 5's built-in assertions (`assertEquals`, `assertTrue`, `assertThrows`) work but produce minimal failure messages. `assertEquals(3, list.size())` fails with "expected 3 but was 5" — but doesn't tell you what was in the list. You add a message parameter, but now every assertion is two lines of boilerplate.

AssertJ's fluent API solves both readability and failure messages: `assertThat(list).hasSize(3)` fails with "Expected size: 3 but was: 5 in: [item1, item2, item3, item4, item5]" — showing the actual content. The assertion reads like a sentence, and the failure message includes context you'd otherwise need to add manually.

AssertJ is not a replacement for JUnit 5 — it's a complement. JUnit handles test lifecycle (`@Test`, `@BeforeEach`, `@ParameterizedTest`). AssertJ handles assertions. Together, they give you the test structure of JUnit and the assertion expressiveness of a dedicated library.

The key advantage: **method chains.** `assertThat(user).isNotNull().extracting(User::getName, User::getEmail).containsExactly("John", "john@test.com")` replaces three separate assertions with one fluent chain. Each chained method narrows the assertion, and any failure shows exactly which condition failed.

sections.title: Collection and Exception Assertions — Where AssertJ Shines Brightest
sections.content:
Collection assertions are where AssertJ's value is most obvious.

```java
assertThat(orders)
    .hasSize(3)
    .extracting(Order::getStatus)
    .containsExactlyInAnyOrder(Status.PENDING, Status.SHIPPED, Status.DELIVERED);

assertThat(users)
    .filteredOn(User::isActive, true)
    .extracting(User::getEmail)
    .contains("active@test.com")
    .doesNotContain("inactive@test.com");
```

`extracting()` pulls a field from each element, turning a `List<Order>` into a list of statuses for easier assertion. `filteredOn()` subsets the collection inline. Compare this to JUnit: you'd need a stream, a collect, and separate assertions.

Exception assertions are equally clean:

```java
assertThatThrownBy(() -> userService.findById(999L))
    .isInstanceOf(UserNotFoundException.class)
    .hasMessage("User 999 not found")
    .hasFieldOrPropertyWithValue("userId", 999L);
```

This replaces JUnit's `assertThrows` + separate message assertion with one fluent chain. The `hasFieldOrPropertyWithValue` check inspects exception fields — useful for custom exceptions with context data.

sections.title: Soft Assertions — Reporting All Failures at Once
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
AssertJ provides a fluent API where assertions read like sentences: `assertThat(list).hasSize(3).contains("item")`. The key advantage over JUnit's `assertEquals` is **failure messages** — AssertJ shows the actual content, not just "expected 3 but was 5."

Collection assertions are where it shines: `extracting(Order::getStatus).containsExactlyInAnyOrder(...)` pulls a field from each element and asserts on the resulting list. This replaces streams, collects, and separate assertions.

Exception assertions chain naturally: `assertThatThrownBy(() -> ...).isInstanceOf(UserNotFoundException.class).hasMessage(...)` — one fluent chain instead of JUnit's `assertThrows` plus separate message checks.

Soft assertions collect all failures and report them at once — fix three bugs in one test run instead of three. Use them for independent field checks like DTO mapping verification.

sections.title: 10 Copy-Pasted Test Methods for 10 Inputs Is a Maintenance Nightmare — Parameterize It
sections.content:
When you need to test the same logic with different inputs, the naive approach is copying the test method 10 times and changing the input value. This creates 10 nearly identical methods that must all be updated when the logic changes. `@ParameterizedTest` runs the same test method with different inputs, replacing 10 methods with one.

JUnit 5 provides multiple sources for parameters: `@ValueSource` for single-type primitives, `@CsvSource` for multi-column data, `@EnumSource` for enum values, and `@MethodSource` for complex objects. Each source feeds rows of data into the test method, and JUnit reports each row as a separate test case with a descriptive name.

The real power isn't reducing line count — it's **revealing patterns.** When you see all inputs and expected outputs together, edge cases become visible. Adding a new test case is one line, not copying an entire method. And when the assertion logic changes, you change it in one place.

Beyond reducing code duplication, parameterized tests improve **test documentation.** When all valid and invalid inputs are listed in one place, the test becomes a specification of the method's behavior. A new developer reads the `@CsvSource` or `@MethodSource` and immediately understands all the cases the method handles. Adding a new edge case is one line, not a new method with setup, act, and assert boilerplate. JUnit 5 reports each parameter set as a separate test case, so failures pinpoint the exact failing input without extra debugging.

The real value isn't less code — it's **revealing edge cases.** When all inputs and expected outputs are listed together, gaps become obvious. Adding a new test case is one line instead of copying a method.

`@MethodSource` methods must be `static` and return `Stream<Arguments>`. Use descriptive names — they appear in test reports, and a failed parameterized test must immediately show which combination failed.

`assertThrows` returns the caught exception for further assertions — message, cause, custom fields. AssertJ's `assertThatThrownBy` chains these fluently: `.isInstanceOf(ValidationException.class).hasMessageContaining("email").hasCauseInstanceOf(DataAccessException.class)`.

Two things most people miss: `hasMessageContaining()` is more resilient than exact message matching, and `assertDoesNotThrow()` explicitly tests that valid input doesn't throw. The negative test is as important as the positive one.

For services that wrap exceptions, `hasCauseInstanceOf()` verifies the wrapping chain — that your service caught the database error and wrapped it in a domain exception.

- **`assertDoesNotThrow()` is the negative test** — explicitly verifies that valid input doesn't throw; equally important as testing that invalid input does throw.

sections.title: A Good Test Is a Specification — A Bad Test Is a Maintenance Burden
sections.content:
Unit tests serve two purposes: **catching regressions** and **documenting behavior.** A test named `testMethod1` that asserts on random implementation details catches regressions poorly (breaks on any refactor) and documents nothing. A test named `shouldRejectOrderWhenInventoryInsufficient` that tests behavior through the public API catches real bugs and serves as executable documentation.

Three principles separate maintainable tests from fragile ones:

**Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA):** Every test has three distinct sections. Arrange sets up the test data and mocks. Act calls the method under test. Assert verifies the result. Clear separation makes tests readable at a glance. When a test mixes setup, execution, and verification in interleaved calls, no one can tell what's being tested.

**Test isolation:** Each test must be independent — runnable alone, in any order, without shared state. Tests that depend on execution order (test A creates data that test B reads) are the most common source of flaky tests. Use `@BeforeEach` for setup, not class-level mutable fields that survive between tests.

**Behavior over implementation:** Test what the code does, not how it does it. If you test that a service calls `repository.save()` followed by `cache.put()` in exactly that order, every refactoring breaks the test. If you test that after creating a user, the user is retrievable and a notification was sent — that's behavior.

How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Good tests follow three principles. **Arrange-Act-Assert** gives each test a clear structure — setup, execution, verification. **Test isolation** means each test runs independently with no shared mutable state — `@BeforeEach` initializes everything fresh. **Behavior over implementation** means testing what the code does, not how it does it.

Naming matters more than people think. `shouldRejectOrderWhenInventoryInsufficient` tells you what broke without reading the test. `testMethod1` tells you nothing.

The one logical assertion guideline: each test verifies one behavior. Multiple `assertThat` calls are fine if they verify the same behavior. But discount AND notification AND logging in one test means three behaviors — split into three tests so failures are immediately diagnosable.

Flaky tests almost always come from shared mutable state. Fresh mocks, fresh data, fresh service instances per test — that's isolation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Arrange-Act-Assert gives tests clear structure** — mixing setup, execution, and verification makes tests unreadable; three distinct sections make the test scannable at a glance.
- **Test behavior, not implementation** — testing that `save()` is called before `cache.put()` breaks on every refactor; testing that the user is retrievable and notified survives implementation changes.
- **One logical assertion per test** — multiple `assertThat` for the same behavior is fine; testing discount + notification + logging in one test makes failures ambiguous; split into focused tests.
- **`@BeforeEach` for isolation, not `@AfterEach`** — if a test fails midway, `@AfterEach` cleanup may not run; initialize fresh state before each test instead of cleaning up after.
- **Flaky tests = shared mutable state** — class-level fields, database rows, static singletons; `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` creates fresh mocks per test; `@DataJpaTest` rolls back transactions.
